claims.text: The untreated W–Cu composite is prone to interfacial phase separation and void formation under service conditions.
A Ni coating approximately 50 nm thick can be deposited on W surfaces by room-temperature magnetron sputtering.
The coated composite is to be annealed at approximately 900 °C for 1 hour in an inert atmosphere.
A slow annealing ramp will permit controlled interdiffusion while avoiding thick, thermally resistive intermetallic compounds.
Sputtering and annealing will create a graded, Ni-rich interfacial layer.
Ni in the interfacial layer will diffuse gradually into both W and Cu.
The graded Ni-rich layer will reduce interfacial energy mismatches and form a stable, continuous transition zone.
The Ni layer will improve wettability at the W–Cu interface.
The graded interface will inhibit diffusion-driven phase separation and void nucleation.
Suppressing phase separation and void nucleation will preserve a continuous heat-conduction path during thermal cycling and irradiation.
The treated composite will have higher thermal conductivity than the untreated W–Cu composite.
The treated composite will contain fewer interfacial voids and phase-separated regions than the untreated composite.
The Ni-modified interface will remain stable under thermal and irradiation stresses relevant to W-based plasma-facing material/Cu-based cooling-component joints.
The intervention is applicable to powder-metallurgy W–Cu composites at service temperatures up to approximately 900 °C.
The intervention is expected to remain effective under moderate irradiation fluxes.
Excessively thick intermetallic compounds formed at the interface could impair thermal conduction.
